Guideline card CO-COHb: Laboratory determination of carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) in blood: specimen, methods and quality control
Independent scientific synthesis based on the references below. Not an official methodology; check the requirements of your laboratory and jurisdiction.
This translation is a draft and has not been reviewed by a specialist yet.
Specimen and factors affecting the result
Interpretation: the limits of a COHb result

Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb); exposure is usually expressed as the fraction of haemoglobin present as COHb (%COHb) [1].

Measurement rests on two principles:
• optical — COHb, oxyhaemoglobin and reduced haemoglobin have different visible spectra, and the fractions are calculated from absorbance values [1][2];
• gas chromatographic — CO is liberated from haemoglobin with a reagent (e.g. acid or potassium hexacyanoferrate(III)) and measured in the headspace above the sample [3][4].

Pulse oximetry does not measure COHb: readings remained high across the range of COHb saturations and failed to detect the fall in measured oxyhaemoglobin saturation, so pulse oximetry is considered unreliable until COHb has been measured directly [5].

The card covers the analytical part of determining COHb in blood: specimen requirements, methods, their limitations and quality control. Both samples from living persons and postmortem samples are included [1][6].

Cases in which ordinary blood is not available (decomposed, formalin-fixed, embalmed, exhumed or fire-dried material) need a separate approach, and the usual COHb methods frequently fail there [7].

The card gives no toxic or lethal levels, threshold tables, treatment or antidote guidance; interpreting the result is the task of a qualified expert.

• CO-oximetry (multiwavelength spectrophotometry). Automated devices estimate total haemoglobin, oxyhaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin fractions simultaneously and are recommended for most clinical purposes [1]. In postmortem whole blood, CO-oximetry measuring at 128 wavelengths was applied to a small sample aliquot and compared with a gas chromatographic method [6].
• Classical spectrophotometric methods. Simple methods based on differential protein precipitation or sodium dithionite reduction are prone to interference from other haemoglobin pigments and imprecise at low levels [1]. Absorbance-difference measurement at isosbestic points for oxy-, carboxy- and reduced haemoglobin with a methaemoglobin correction is described, as is qualitative confirmation by spectral detail, dithionite reduction and first-derivative spectra [2].
• Gas chromatography. Releasing and measuring CO is required for low-level exposure and for postmortem samples in which putrefaction or heat stress has changed haemoglobin composition [1]. Detectors include capillary GC with a micro thermal conductivity detector [3]; catalytic reduction of CO to methane with FID (iron determined by atomic absorption spectrophotometry) [6]; and automated headspace GC/MS [4][8]. Adding sodium dithionite in GC methods reduces methaemoglobin to haemoglobin and removes the resulting error [9].
• Quality control. Calibration and controls at known levels are used, and fitness for the intended purpose is demonstrated by validation [10][11]. Working range, linearity, accuracy and precision are assessed [12]. In method comparison, Bland-Altman analysis and interlaboratory proficiency testing were used, with accuracy reported as bias and precision as relative standard deviation [6]. A reliable analytical result is the precondition for interpretation [11].

A short comparison of the three approaches:
• CO-oximetry (multiwavelength): fast, small volume, several haemoglobin fractions in one measurement, recommended for most clinical purposes [1]; but error is possible in the low saturation range and in the presence of other haemoglobin pigments — in a comparison study one sample in the lower range was false negative and individual samples at high saturation deviated markedly [6].
• Classical spectrophotometric methods (differential protein precipitation, dithionite reduction): simple and inexpensive, but prone to interference and imprecise at low levels [1]; absorbance differences at isosbestic points with a methaemoglobin correction improve accuracy, yet accuracy is diminished in denatured or autolysed blood while identification remains reliable [2].
• Gas chromatography (release and measurement of CO): required for low-level exposure and for postmortem-altered material [1]; it has worked with putrefied and thermocoagulated samples [4][8] and agreed satisfactorily with CO-oximetry over the whole measured range [6]; but computing %COHb from the ratio of saturated to unsaturated blood errs when methaemoglobin is present, hence the addition of dithionite [9].

• CO-oximetry is fast, works on a small blood volume and yields several haemoglobin fractions in one measurement [1][6].
• Gas chromatographic methods have also been applied to putrefied, heat-affected and contaminated material: automated headspace GC/MS worked with blood and bone-marrow aspirates and confirmed CO-oximeter findings [4]; in putrid postmortem blood GC/MS showed a linear response and good reproducibility [8].
• Capillary GC with a micro thermal conductivity detector offers high resolution and a short analysis time, and CO release with acid was gradual and reproducible [3].
• When ordinary blood is unavailable, carboxy-haem saturation can be calculated by measuring CO by GC/MS and iron by flame atomic absorption spectrophotometry in the same aliquot [7].
• In postmortem blood collected in vacutainer tubes with or without preservative and kept refrigerated, COHb was found to be stable over long-term storage [13].

• Optical methods are sensitive to other haemoglobin pigments: analysis of postmortem blood is often biased by pigments such as methaemoglobin and sulfhaemoglobin [2], and simple spectrophotometric methods are prone to interference and imprecise at low levels [1].
• On heating, haemoglobin forms differ in heat susceptibility and precipitability; absorbance spectra of heated samples deteriorate, double-wavelength spectrophotometry gives a wrong %COHb, an artificial increase of %COHb occurs, and CO is also produced spontaneously during heating [14].
• In postmortem cases the spectrophotometric COHb result may be inaccurate when the sample or the analysis is inadequate [15].
• Methaemoglobin does not bind CO, so GC methods that compute %COHb from the ratio of unsaturated to CO-saturated blood give erroneously high values [9].
• In a method comparison the overall agreement was satisfactory, yet individual samples at high saturation deviated markedly and one sample in the lower range was false negative by CO-oximetry [6].
• Changes in the optical state and degradation of blood during sampling, transport and storage strongly affect spectrophotometric analysis [16].

• Specimen type and collection. Blood is collected into a tube with an anticoagulant (or preservative); separate recommendations exist for the collection, amounts, preservatives and storage conditions of forensic toxicology specimens [17]. The tube is filled, leaving minimal headspace, sealed and refrigerated: storage temperature, preservative, time, tube headspace volume, initial saturation and freeze-thaw and reopening cycles have been studied as factors affecting the COHb result [16]. In refrigerated vacutainer tubes COHb was found to be stable [13].
• Postmortem changes. Putrefaction and heat alter haemoglobin composition, and such samples call for a gas chromatographic method [1]. Headspace GC/MS has been applied to thermocoagulated and putrefied material [4][8]. Heating can artificially raise %COHb [14].
• Appearance. Cherry-red or pink lividity is described with carbon monoxide but also with hypothermia and cyanide poisoning, so it is not specific and does not replace laboratory measurement [18].
• Physiological and exposure factors. CO is a non-specific marker of tobacco exposure; exhaled CO correlates closely with blood COHb, but elimination varies with sex, ventilation, exercise and time of day, and several non-smoking conditions raise CO [19]. Under oxygen administration the decline of COHb was described by a bi-compartmental rather than a mono-compartmental model, with a slight rebound after oxygen was stopped [20].

A %COHb figure on its own never firmly establishes the severity of poisoning or the cause of death. A general rule of postmortem toxicology is that a concentration is not interpreted in isolation [21]; compilations and tables of "lethal concentrations" are regarded as misleading [22][23], and a result is considered together with the antemortem history and other information [23]. Postmortem changes invalidate clinical pharmacokinetic assumptions [22], and the preanalytic phase and specimen quality govern what a result means [24].

Interpretation weighs at least the following together: the condition of the specimen (postmortem changes, putrefaction, heat or burns, storage conditions and tube headspace) [16][14][1]; the laboratory method used and its interferences (CO-oximetry in postmortem or haemolysed blood, other haemoglobin species) [6][2][9][15]; the time since exposure and oxygen administration [20]; smoking and other sources of CO [19]; and other evidence such as autopsy, scene and history [23][18]. Only a qualified expert draws the conclusion; the card gives no toxic or lethal levels and no severity tables.

• A COHb result is not a conclusion in itself. Only a qualified expert evaluates it together with the circumstances of the event, smoking and other CO sources [19], the time since exposure and oxygen administration [20], and the condition and storage of the specimen [16][14]. The card gives no toxic or lethal levels.
• Do not rely on a single method: confirming a spectrophotometric result with a second technique based on a different analytical principle is considered essential [9].
• An inadequate sample or an altered optical state can make the result inaccurate and lead to misclassification of the role of CO [15].
• In the clinical setting a pulse oximeter reading does not replace a COHb measurement [5].
• The colour of lividity and other external signs are not specific [18].
• Reliable interpretation presupposes analytical reliability: method validation and quality control are an integral part of the report [11][10].

• Releasing CO and measuring it by gas chromatography serves as the confirmatory (reference) approach, and comparing a spectrophotometric result with a GC method based on a different principle is recommended [9][1]. In postmortem whole blood, CO-oximetry and headspace GC-FID (with iron by atomic absorption spectrophotometry) agreed satisfactorily over the whole measured range [6].
• Measuring total blood CO (haemoglobin-bound plus dissociated) by headspace GC-MS has been proposed as a separate approach, from which COHb can be estimated [15]. Under non-optimal storage, total CO proved more stable than COHb [16].
• When ordinary blood is unavailable, other material is used: bone-marrow aspirate [4]; spleen, liver, muscle, dried blood and decomposed tissue [7].
• The choice of specimens and methods, the difference between screening and confirmatory analysis and validation requirements are covered in separate cards [11][10][17].
